title: AppLocker Enforced Application Blocks (Events 8004 and 8007)
exclusions: This rule reports AppLocker enforce-mode blocks: Event ID 8004 from the EXE and DLL channel and Event ID 8007 from the MSI and Script channel. It does not include AppLocker audit-only would-block events 8003/8006, allowed events, policy-application failures, packaged-app channels, or policy edits. Despite the historical title, it does not detect Windows Defender Application Control/App Control for Business CodeIntegrity events such as enforced block 3077, audit event 3076, signature event 3089, or policy-load event 3099. A block does not prove malware, malicious intent, successful execution, or an ATT&CK technique. Collection gaps, disabled channels, unsupported Windows editions, applications outside enabled rule collections, and activity before coverage remain invisible. No regulation or runtime assurance is claimed.
evidence: After deployment, retain the version-controlled `windows_applocker_enforced_blocks` saved-search definition and ACL; schedule, dispatch, and triggered-alert history; each result with endpoint, event ID, channel, target user/logon ID, policy/rule identity, full file path, EventRecordID, source, and source type; matching raw AppLocker XML; effective AppLocker policy and enforcement mode; input/add-on version; channel/source-health results; dated positive and negative controls; alert delivery; analyst disposition; and bounded exception approval. This documentation-only review generated no AppLocker event, Splunk job, alert, or production evidence.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated test index and fixed time range, replay two XML fixtures. Fixture A has `source=XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/EXE and DLL`, `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog`, `EventCode=8004`, `Computer=WIN-APPLOCKER.example`, `EventRecordID=34001`, and `UserData_Xml` values `PolicyName=EXE`, `RuleId={11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111}`, `RuleName=Block unsigned tools`, `TargetUser=EXAMPLE\alice`, `TargetLogonId=0x1234`, `FullFilePath=C:\Users\alice\Downloads\tool.exe`. Fixture B uses the MSI and Script source, EventCode 8007, EventRecordID 34002, PolicyName `Script`, and path `C:\Users\alice\Downloads\run.ps1`. Expect exactly two rows with block types `EXE or DLL blocked` and `Script or MSI blocked`, preserving the two record IDs and paths. Documentation review checks logic only; replay was not performed.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Run isolated variants and expect zero rows for each: AppLocker audit-only Event IDs 8003 and 8006; allowed IDs 8002 and 8005; CodeIntegrity Event ID 3077; Event ID 8004 under the MSI and Script source; Event ID 8007 under EXE and DLL; either ID in `XmlWinEventLog:Security`; Classic-rendered events under another source type; malformed nonnumeric event IDs; empty endpoint identity; events at or after the exclusive latest boundary; and events outside the selected closed hour. A valid 8004 with an empty RuleName but populated RuleId and FullFilePath must still return one row.

dataSources: Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/EXE and DLL Event ID 8004 and Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/MSI and Script Event ID 8007 from in-scope Windows endpoints, collected in XML by Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742) version 10.0.1. The deployment-local example uses `index=wineventlog`; expected contracts are `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog` with source `XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/EXE and DLL` or `XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/MSI and Script`. Parse `UserData_Xml` and verify `PolicyName`, `RuleId`, `RuleName`, `RuleSddl`, `TargetUser`, `TargetLogonId`, and `FullFilePath`, plus `Computer`, `EventCode` or `EventID`, and `EventRecordID`.
app: Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742), version 10.0.1, for XML Windows Event Log collection and field knowledge. Splunkbase lists that release for Splunk Enterprise 9.3 through current 10.x releases and Splunk Cloud at review time. Test upgrades, especially from releases before the documented 5.0.0 breaking-change boundary. No premium app is required.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog" (source="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/EXE and DLL" OR source="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/MSI and Script") (EventCode=8004 OR EventCode=8007) earliest=-70m@m latest=-10m@m
| spath input=UserData_Xml
| rename RuleAndFileData.* as *
| eval event_code=tonumber(coalesce(EventCode,EventID)), endpoint=lower(trim(coalesce(dest,Computer,host))), file_path=trim(coalesce(FullFilePath,FilePath)), target_user=trim(coalesce(TargetUser,UserName,user)), rule_id=trim(coalesce(RuleId,RuleNameOrId)), rule_name=trim(RuleName)
| where (event_code=8004 AND source="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/EXE and DLL" OR event_code=8007 AND source="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/MSI and Script") AND len(endpoint)>0
| eval block_type=if(event_code=8004,"EXE or DLL blocked","Script or MSI blocked"), detection="AppLocker enforce-mode application block"
| table _time endpoint event_code block_type target_user TargetLogonId PolicyName rule_id rule_name RuleSddl file_path EventRecordID detection source sourcetype
| sort 0 -_time endpoint event_code file_path
description: Reports one row per AppLocker enforce-mode block in the delayed closed hour: Event 8004 for an EXE or DLL, or Event 8007 for a script or Windows Installer file. Each row is at blocked-file event grain and retains endpoint, user/logon context, policy and rule identifiers, path, channel, and event-record identity.
value: Reviewing every enforced application-control denial helps responders distinguish prevented unauthorized execution from broken software deployment, repair unsafe policy gaps without weakening controls, and identify repeated attempts against sensitive endpoints while preserving proof that Windows blocked the file.
implementation: Enable and govern the required AppLocker rule collections and enforce mode, then collect both AppLocker channels in XML with Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows 10.0.1. Validate `UserData_Xml` parsing before saving `windows_applocker_enforced_blocks`. Run hourly over `-70m@m` to `-10m@m` and trigger on any row; enrich and prioritize after the base result by asset criticality, file reputation, user context, repeat attempts, and approved deployment state.
visualization: On an application-control dashboard, place endpoint/channel freshness and AppLocker policy coverage first. Add single values for blocked endpoints and files; a time chart split by 8004/8007; bars by PolicyName, rule, and target user; and a table with endpoint, block type, full path, user/logon ID, rule ID/name, EventRecordID, owner, ticket, and disposition. Drill down to raw XML, effective AppLocker policy, file hash/signature telemetry from a companion source, process lineage, software deployment records, and repeated attempts. Do not label a path malicious from this event alone.
schema: Native Microsoft AppLocker XML event fields; no lossless Splunk CIM dataset is claimed
dataModelAcceleration: No `cimSpl` is supplied. Splunk's AppLocker guidance notes that the required AppLocker detail is not specifically mapped to CIM, and a generic Change or Endpoint query cannot be assumed to retain channel, EventRecordID, RuleId, TargetLogonId, and FullFilePath. Keep raw XML as the detection and evidence contract. A local summary may be built only after fixed-window row and field parity tests.

knownFalsePositives:
A result is a genuine AppLocker enforced block. “False positive” means the denial is expected or benign for security triage, not that the block did not happen.

1. **Approved software deployment omitted from policy** — Microsoft Configuration Manager, Intune, Group Policy startup scripts, or an enterprise deployment tool may invoke a new signed installer, executable, or script before its publisher/hash/path rule is deployed. Verify package ID, signer/hash from companion telemetry, deployment ring, endpoint, target user, exact path, ticket, and policy version. Fix sequencing; do not globally allow the deployment directory.

2. **Application update changed hash, signer chain, or path** — Browser, agent, runtime, or line-of-business updates can invalidate narrow rules. Confirm vendor release, package signature, expected install path, software owner, and before/after policy test. Add the least-broad publisher/file rule approved by the policy owner; never allow `%TEMP%` or a user-writable tree as a shortcut.

3. **Administrator or support diagnostic tool** — An authorized engineer may try an unsigned or unapproved utility from Downloads or a support directory. Correlate access request, operator, host, file hash/signature, source, and maintenance bounds. Treat repeated attempts after denial as a separate concern, and use a finite targeted approval rather than suppressing all administrator activity.

4. **Logon, build, or configuration script not represented in policy** — A newly introduced PowerShell, batch, VBScript, JavaScript, or MSI can produce 8007. Match script repository commit, code-signing identity, deployment manifest, target group, and approved window. A familiar filename alone is insufficient because user-writable script paths are replaceable.

5. **AppLocker policy rollout or rule-collection transition** — Moving from Audit only to Enforce rules or changing GPO scope can expose latent incompatibilities across many endpoints. Confirm GPO GUID/version, Resultant Set of Policy, rollout ring, expected blocked manifest, and rollback criteria. Suppress notification only for exact expected files/endpoints during the finite rollout; preserve every block for safety review.

6. **Purple-team or application-control validation** — An approved control test should intentionally produce 8004 or 8007. Match engagement/test ID, operator, target list, exact file hash/path, UTC interval, and expected rule. Keep the first alert as control evidence and suppress only duplicate notifications inside the approved interval.

**Safe suppression:** preserve the base result and raw event. In an alert wrapper, use a governed lookup keyed on endpoint, event_code, normalized exact file path or immutable hash from companion telemetry, rule_id, target user where necessary, `valid_from_epoch`, `valid_until_epoch`, owner, and ticket. Suppress notification only when every populated key and current time match. Reject wildcard user-writable paths, endpoint-wide exceptions, administrator-only allowlists, unsigned filename-only entries, and open-ended dates. Revalidate after policy, OS, add-on, or application updates.
mitreAttack: N/A (AppLocker block events are control outcomes and do not identify one adversary technique)

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and event contract

Assign an application-control policy owner, endpoint engineering owner, software-deployment owner, Splunk collection owner, SOC detection owner, responder, and exception approver. Inventory in-scope Windows versions, editions, endpoints, AppLocker GPOs/local policies, rule collections, enforcement modes, and authoritative software catalog. AppLocker coverage is not inferred from event presence: document whether EXE, DLL, Script, and Windows Installer collections are enabled and whether each is Audit only or Enforce rules.

Install Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742) version 10.0.1 on the required collection, parsing, and search tiers. Splunkbase lists Splunk Enterprise 9.3 through current 10.x and Cloud support at review time. Test exact OS, Universal Forwarder, add-on, and Splunk versions and follow upgrade instructions when crossing the 5.0.0 breaking-change boundary.

The collector account needs permission to read both AppLocker operational channels. The search role needs read access to the deployment-local `wineventlog` index and permission to save/schedule the search; it does not need AppLocker policy-edit, endpoint-administrator, software-deployment, or exception-lookup-write access. Restrict file paths, usernames, rule SDDL, and raw endpoint events.

Microsoft documents 8004 as an EXE/DLL prevented from running in Enforce rules mode and 8007 as a script/MSI prevented from running in Enforce rules mode. Audit-only counterparts 8003 and 8006 mean the file ran but would be blocked under enforcement. Do not mix them: this UC answers “what Windows says it blocked,” not “what policy would block.” It also does not cover App Control for Business/WDAC CodeIntegrity 3077. Implement those events as a separate control with their distinct channel, fields, semantics, and tests.

No count threshold applies: one admitted block is one reviewable event. Notification priority may later consider endpoint criticality, file trust, repeated attempts, and deployment context. A block is prevention evidence, not proof that the file is malicious or that another execution path did not succeed.

## Step 1 — Collect and verify both AppLocker channels

Create governed inputs in an app's `local/inputs.conf`, not the add-on's `default` directory:

```ini
[WinEventLog://Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/EXE and DLL]
disabled = 0
renderXml = true
index = wineventlog
checkpointInterval = 5

[WinEventLog://Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/MSI and Script]
disabled = 0
renderXml = true
index = wineventlog
checkpointInterval = 5
```

`wineventlog` is a deployment-local index choice. Record actual `current_only`, `start_from`, checkpoint, allow/deny filters, forwarding route, and retention. Do not filter out 8004/8007 at collection time. Validate effective configuration with `splunk btool inputs list --debug`, forwarder health, and protected transport. If using WEF/WEC, collect each channel, preserve original Computer and EventRecordID, measure delay, and prevent duplicate direct and forwarded inputs.

Verify source contracts and XML payload before enabling the alert:

```spl
index=wineventlog sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog (source="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/EXE and DLL" OR source="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/MSI and Script") (EventCode=8004 OR EventCode=8007) earliest=-30d
| spath input=UserData_Xml
| rename RuleAndFileData.* as *
| table _time Computer EventCode EventRecordID PolicyName RuleId RuleName RuleSddl TargetUser TargetLogonId FullFilePath source
| head 100
```

Compare selected records with Event Viewer under **Applications and Services Logs > Microsoft > Windows > AppLocker**. Confirm event ID/channel pairing, endpoint, record ID, target token, policy/rule identity, and full path. `UserData_Xml` shape can vary with collection and Windows versions; inspect raw XML rather than inventing fields. Keep the explicit `spath`/rename only after proving the `RuleAndFileData` path. If the add-on already extracts flat fields, prove that applying it does not overwrite values.

Build source-health coverage for both expected channels on every in-scope endpoint. These block events are activity-driven and may legitimately be absent, so use forwarder/channel freshness and controlled telemetry, not a requirement for recent blocks. Compare the endpoint inventory to collected Computer values and report missing channels separately.

## Step 2 — Save and understand the search

Save the SPL as `windows_applocker_enforced_blocks`. Schedule hourly, such as `5 * * * *`, using embedded `earliest=-70m@m latest=-10m@m`. This is a nonoverlapping closed 60-minute event-time window delayed ten minutes. Measure p99 `_indextime-_time`; if latency requires more delay, shift both bounds equally and preserve the 60-minute width.

The base clause admits only the XML source type, two exact source channels, and IDs 8004/8007. `spath` parses the XML payload and `rename RuleAndFileData.* as *` exposes Microsoft's event fields. The evaluations normalize numeric event ID, endpoint, path, target user, and rule identity while retaining originals. The `where` clause reasserts valid ID/channel combinations and rejects empty endpoints. Parentheses are material: 8004 belongs to EXE and DLL, while 8007 belongs to MSI and Script.

`block_type` describes Microsoft semantics without guessing the exact file extension. The table remains one source event per row and retains EventRecordID for provenance. Do not aggregate away channel, user, rule, or path in the alert result. If repeat attempts are needed, add a secondary correlation search keyed on endpoint, user, normalized path/hash, and a documented time window.

No `cimSpl` is claimed. A generic Change model does not preserve this event contract, and application-control blocks are not policy-change events. Splunk's AppLocker guidance parses native XML detail directly. If a local accelerated dataset is created, constrain the exact events and prove row count and all required fields against raw XML over fixed windows, including acceleration lag.

## Step 3 — Validate boundaries and semantics

Replay the two positive XML fixtures in an isolated index using fixed event times inside the search bounds. Assert exactly two rows and exact endpoint, event ID, block type, target user/logon ID, PolicyName, RuleId/RuleName, path, EventRecordID, source, and source type. Add separate fixtures for blank optional RuleName, path containing spaces, domain-qualified user, and both EventCode and EventID extraction variants.

Run every negative variant independently: audit-only and allowed IDs, CodeIntegrity 3077, swapped source/ID pairs, Security source, Classic source type, malformed event code, empty endpoint, latest-boundary exclusion, and outside-window events. Test earliest inclusion. If duplicate WEF/direct records appear with the same Computer/source/EventRecordID, fix collection topology; do not add broad `dedup` until provenance and collision behavior are understood.

In an approved disposable Windows lab, export the effective AppLocker policy, confirm Enforce rules for the test collection, and execute a harmless test EXE/DLL or script/MSI that a dedicated rule blocks. Do not use malware. Verify Event Viewer first, then Splunk field parity, one result, alert delivery, and dashboard drilldown. Restore the prior test policy and remove the file. Separately switch a lab collection to Audit only and prove that 8003/8006 do not enter this rule.

Record policy XML/GPO version, OS/forwarder/add-on/Splunk versions, effective input, UTC bounds, fixture hashes, lab command and file hash, expected and actual rows, search job ID, alert receipt, cleanup, and owner acceptance. Keep `status=draft` until source coverage, parsing, event semantics, boundary tests, notification, dashboard RBAC, response, and exception behavior are human accepted.

## Step 4 — Triage and response

For each row: (1) open raw XML and verify endpoint, channel, ID, EventRecordID, user/logon ID, rule, and full path; (2) confirm effective AppLocker policy and enforcement mode on that endpoint; (3) obtain file hash, signature, prevalence, origin, process ancestry, and attempted command line from approved companion telemetry because AppLocker event fields alone may not provide all of them; (4) compare software catalog and deployment records; (5) determine whether the denial prevented unauthorized activity or broke an authorized workflow; and (6) document disposition and policy/software remediation.

If suspicious, investigate adjacent successful executions, alternate paths, child processes, downloads, persistence, account activity, and other endpoints. Follow incident response based on corroborated behavior. If benign, update the authoritative application-control policy using the narrowest safe signer, publisher, hash, or protected-path rule and staged testing. Never auto-create an allow rule, move the file, disable AppLocker/Application Identity, switch a production collection to Audit only, or allow a user-writable directory from one alert.

Use the dashboard in `visualization` and keep source-health gaps visually distinct from zero blocks. Route blocks on critical assets or repeated unknown files urgently; route known deployment incompatibilities to endpoint engineering while retaining security visibility. Review finite exceptions at least monthly and after policy, software, signer, or OS changes.

## Step 5 — Troubleshooting

- **No events after a lab block:** verify the correct rule collection is Enforce rules, Application Identity/AppLocker prerequisites, Event Viewer channel, exact input stanza, forwarder route, and index permissions.
- **8003/8006 appear but no 8004/8007:** the collection is Audit only or the tested rule is not enforced. Do not relabel would-block events as blocks.
- **WDAC 3077 is missing:** expected; it belongs to Microsoft-Windows-CodeIntegrity/Operational and is excluded from this AppLocker rule.
- **Fields are null:** inspect raw `UserData_Xml`, XML namespace/path, add-on placement/version, and search app context. Adjust `spath` only from observed XML and rerun fixtures.
- **Wrong source type:** version 6+ XML collection uses `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog` and channel-bearing `source`. Correct ingestion instead of widening to ambiguous Classic values.
- **Many blocks during rollout:** compare exact GPO version, endpoint ring, file manifest, and deployment order. Preserve events and use finite, exact notification exceptions.
- **A supposedly allowed file is blocked:** verify Resultant Set of Policy, rule collection, user/group token, publisher/signature chain, path expansion, policy merge, and rule precedence on the affected endpoint.
- **Duplicate rows:** check direct plus WEF/WEC collection and Computer/source/EventRecordID. Repair topology before considering event-identity deduplication.
- **Late records miss the hour:** measure clocks, WEF delay, queues, `_indextime-_time`, and scheduler dispatch. Shift both bounds together.
- **Alert says malware:** fix downstream wording. This control reports a policy block; maliciousness requires corroborating file and behavior evidence.
grandmaExplanation: We show when Windows refuses to run a program, script, or installer because it breaks the organization's approved-software rules. The team can then decide whether it stopped something dangerous or accidentally blocked legitimate work.
hardware: Supported Windows clients and servers where AppLocker is available and the relevant EXE/DLL and MSI/Script rule collections are configured. DLL collection is not enabled by default and can be high volume. For WEF/WEC, preserve original Computer, source channel, EventRecordID, and XML payload and prevent duplicate direct collection.
